thread: It's Taco Tuesday. Here's how to tell whether a taco place is actually good, before you order:

Look for tortillas made there.

Fresh corn tortillas, pressed and griddled to order, are the biggest difference between a good taco and a forgettable one. If you can see someone pressing tortillas, you're in the right place.

Count the fillings.

The best taquerias sell five or six. A 40-item menu with burgers on it means the kitchen isn't built around tacos.

Check the salsa.

Three or four house-made salsas at different heat levels means the kitchen cares. One squeeze bottle of store-bought hot sauce means it doesn't.

And if there's a vertical spit of marinated pork in view, order al pastor. It's the hardest taco on the menu to fake.

What else to order, and how to find good tacos near you: https://www.savorscout.net/food/tacos

Picking a restaurant for eight people shouldn't take a 90-minute group chat.

Past about six people, it stops being about taste. It's logistics. Here's what actually matters:

Ask for one long table when you book.

Split across two tables, you've basically had two separate dinners. Restaurants will tell you honestly whether they can do it if you ask first.

Pick a place with shared plates.

Eight separate orders come out at eight different times. Shared plates fix the pace, the service and the bill at once.

Pick a menu with cheap and pricey dishes, and go somewhere a little loud.

Someone's always on a budget. And in a quiet room, your group becomes the loudest thing in it.

And don't put it to an open vote in the group chat. Give everyone one veto instead.

That's how SavorScout rooms work: one link, everyone taps yes on anything they'd eat, one veto each. https://www.savorscout.net/what-to-eat/big-group
Not sure what to order at a ramen shop? Start with the broth. There are four main kinds:

Tonkotsu: pork bone broth, simmered until it's rich and cloudy. The heaviest and most famous style.

Shoyu: a clearer chicken or pork broth seasoned with soy sauce. Lighter and more savory.

Miso: seasoned with fermented soybean paste. Sweeter and nuttier, usually with corn and butter.

Shio: salt-based, and the lightest of the four. It's the hardest to make well, so it's the best test of a serious shop.
Two more signs of a good bowl: the broth coats your spoon instead of running straight off, and the egg has a jammy, runny center. A hard-boiled egg tells you what kind of kitchen it is.

And pick a shop that mostly sells ramen. A place with 40 other dishes on the menu isn't simmering pork bones for 12 hours.

More on ordering ramen: https://www.savorscout.net/food/ramen

It's National Sandwich Day, so here's how to tell a sandwich shop is actually good before you order.

Look for a meat slicer running behind the counter. Pre-sliced deli meat goes leathery within hours. The bread should taste like something and hold together without scraping the roof of your mouth. And there should be something sharp inside, like pickles or pickled onions.
